turns.text: The way he just stopped trying. I kept making excuses for him, thinking things would get better. Now I keep wishing I’d left sooner.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It hurts to look back and blame yourself, but you were hoping for something you cared about. You made the best sense you could of things at the time. What do you wish you could say to yourself back then?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I wish I could tell myself that I shouldn’t have to beg someone to care. But I still miss him, and that makes me feel pathetic.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Missing him doesn’t make you pathetic. You can know you deserved more and still grieve the person and the hope you had. That’s a painful place to be.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah. I miss who I thought he was, I think. And I hate that some part of me still wants him to come back and say he’s sorry.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That longing makes sense—you’re grieving the person you believed he could be, and wishing he’d recognize the hurt he caused. You don’t have to judge yourself for wanting that.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep checking my phone, even though I know he probably won’t text. Then I feel stupid all over again. It’s like I can’t stop hoping.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That hope can keep tugging at you, even when another part of you knows what to expect. Checking your phone may be your way of reaching for some relief or closure. What do you find yourself hoping his message would give you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want him to admit he hurt me. To say it wasn’t because I wasn’t enough. I don’t know if hearing that from him would even help, though.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Wanting him to acknowledge the hurt—and to know it wasn’t a measure of your worth—makes sense. And you’re unsure whether he could give you the relief you need. What feels most important for you to hear right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I just feel awful about how I look lately. Like… I don’t even want people to see me.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds really painful, like being seen feels hard right now. I’m glad you told me. Are you thinking of ending your life? You can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No… I’m not thinking about ending my life. I just feel so ashamed of my body. I’ve gained about 30 pounds, and I can barely stand looking at myself.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: I’m glad you’re not thinking about ending your life. It sounds like the shame has gotten really heavy, and I’m sorry you’re carrying it. What feels hardest about being seen right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep thinking everyone notices how much weight I’ve gained. I’ve started avoiding food, too. Yesterday I didn’t eat until 7pm, when I was almost passing out.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds frightening, and avoiding food until you were nearly passing out is serious. You deserve support with this, not judgment. Could you tell someone you trust what’s been happening and reach out to a doctor or counsellor? What feels doable right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don’t know. I’m embarrassed to tell anyone. And I feel like if I eat earlier, I’ll just gain even more.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It makes sense that embarrassment and fear are making this hard to talk about. But nearly passing out is a sign this is affecting your wellbeing, and a doctor or counsellor could help you through it. What worries you most about telling someone?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’m scared they’ll judge me or just tell me to lose weight. I don’t really know how to explain that I’m afraid to eat, not just unhappy with my body.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re worried they’ll focus on your weight and miss how afraid you feel around food. That sounds lonely. You could say, “I’m avoiding food because I’m scared of gaining weight, and yesterday I nearly passed out.” Is there someone you’d feel safest telling?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe my sister. She’s usually kind, but I still feel stupid saying it out loud. I don’t want her to think I’m being dramatic.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It doesn’t sound stupid or dramatic; you’re scared and this is affecting your health. Your sister’s kindness may make her a good person to start with. What might make it feel a little easier to tell her?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don’t even know where to start. Work just stopped, and I have no idea when I’ll get paid again. I’m trying not to panic, but it’s a lot.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds really frightening, especially with no clear idea when money will come in. What feels most urgent or worrying right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The not knowing. I’ve been lucky to have steady work, and now I keep trying to figure out how long I can manage if the checks don’t come. It’s hard to switch my brain off.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: The uncertainty is keeping your mind on high alert, trying to calculate every possible outcome. That sounds exhausting. Has this started affecting your sleep or your day-to-day life?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah, I’m sleeping badly. I wake up in the middle of the night and start doing the math again. During the day I’m distracted, even when I’m trying to be with my family. I feel like I should have a plan, but I don’t know what to plan for.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds like a lot to carry, and it’s spilling into your sleep and time with your family. Since it’s affecting both, talking with a counsellor could help, and we can keep talking here too. What part of the uncertainty feels hardest to sit with?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I think it’s that I can’t tell whether this is a short pause or if everything’s going to change. I’ve worked hard to build some security, and suddenly it feels like I could lose it without any warning. I don’t really know what to do with that fear.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It makes sense that this feels frightening: the work pause has shaken the security you worked hard to build, and you don’t know how long it will last. What would help most right now: space to talk through the fear, or help thinking about one small next step?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I think I need to talk through it a little more. I’m scared I’ll let my family down if the money dries up. And I hate that I can’t give them an answer when they ask what’s going to happen.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re carrying the fear of letting them down, along with the pressure to answer something you genuinely don’t know yet. It sounds painful to feel responsible for giving your family certainty when you don’t have it yourself.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah. I keep thinking I should be able to make this okay somehow, but I can’t control when work comes back. I don’t want my family to see how scared I am.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like you’re trying to protect your family from your fear while carrying something you can’t control. You don’t have to make it okay all at once. What feels hardest about letting them see even a little of how you’re feeling?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep thinking I could do better in school if I were just better at writing. Like, that’s the thing holding me back.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds frustrating to feel like your writing is getting in the way of showing what you know. What part of writing feels hardest for you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I guess getting my thoughts to come out clearly. I know what I mean in my head, but then I write it and it sounds… not smart enough.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That gap between what you mean and what ends up on the page can feel really discouraging. It doesn’t mean your thoughts aren’t smart; it may just be hard to shape them into words.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah. I spend so long trying to make it sound right that I sometimes don’t even finish. Then I feel stupid for not getting it done.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds like a tough loop: trying so hard to make every sentence right that the work stalls, then blaming yourself for it. Taking a first pass that’s allowed to be rough can sometimes make it easier to keep going.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe. I just worry that if I hand in something rough, it’ll prove I’m not good enough. My grades already make me feel like everyone else can do this more easily.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like the rough draft feels risky, as if it might confirm a fear you already have about not measuring up. Grades can make that comparison feel even sharper, but they don’t tell the whole story of what you’re capable of.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I know grades aren’t everything, but I still feel ashamed when I get one back and it’s lower than I expected. I start thinking I should be able to fix this on my own.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That shame sounds heavy, especially when it turns into pressure to solve everything by yourself. You don’t have to figure out what’s making writing hard alone. Would talking with a teacher or writing tutor feel possible?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe a tutor. I’m not sure how to ask without sounding like I’m bad at school.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It makes sense to want help without feeling judged. You could frame it as wanting to get your ideas across more clearly, not as being bad at school. What would feel most comfortable: asking in person or sending a short message?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep thinking I should be doing something that actually matters. But I get through the workday, come home, and feel like I’ve wasted another day.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds exhausting to keep measuring your days against some bigger purpose and come away feeling you’ve fallen short. What does “something that matters” mean to you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don’t know exactly. Just… something I can care about, I guess. Right now I do my tasks, get paid, and try not to think too hard about how little it means to me.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like you’re getting through the routine, but there isn’t much in it that feels like yours. What do you find yourself caring about, even a little, when you’re not trying to make it count?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I used to care about making things. I’d draw, sometimes make little furniture projects. I haven’t done either in ages. Now even thinking about it makes me feel guilty, like I should be using that time to figure out my career instead.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like the things that used to make you feel alive have started to feel like one more test you have to pass. What feels most pressing when you think about your career?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That I’ll wake up years from now and realize I just kept choosing what was safe. I don’t even know what I’d choose instead, though.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re afraid safety could quietly turn into a life you didn’t choose, but there isn’t a clear alternative yet. That’s a hard place to be. What would make a small step toward exploring feel safe enough, without needing to decide your whole career?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe talking to someone who does work I’m curious about. I could ask how they got there. I just feel a little embarrassed that I’m this unsure at my age.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Feeling unsure doesn’t mean you’re behind; it sounds like you’re trying to be honest about what matters to you. Talking with someone could be a gentle way to explore, without committing to a big change. What kind of work are you curious about?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’ve wondered about design work, maybe making things people actually use. But it feels silly to say that when I haven’t drawn in years. I wouldn’t even know how to start.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That doesn’t sound silly; it sounds like an interest you haven’t had room to explore in a while. You don’t have to be ready to call yourself a designer to be curious about the work. What part of making useful things draws you in most?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I guess I’m worried my friends are getting tired of me. They call me a weirdo because I don’t talk much, and I don’t really know how to change that.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like being called a weirdo is making you wonder whether your friends still want you around. What worries you most about how they’re treating you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That they’ll just stop inviting me eventually. Sometimes I can tell they’re annoyed when I don’t join in, but I don’t always know what to say.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds lonely, especially when you want to join in but the words don’t come easily. What usually makes it hardest to speak up in those moments?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I just can’t think of anything to say. Then I start worrying it’ll be awkward, so I stay quiet, and that probably makes them more annoyed.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds like a tough loop: worrying about awkwardness makes it harder to speak, and then you worry your silence is pushing them away. It doesn’t mean you don’t care about them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah. I do care. I just don’t know how to show it without forcing myself to act like someone else.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You want them to know you care, without having to become someone you’re not. What feels most like you when you’re showing someone you care?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe listening, or checking in with one person later. I’m better one-on-one. In a group I just kind of disappear.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like one-on-one is where you can be more yourself, and listening or checking in already shows you care. You don’t have to be the loudest person in the group for that to count.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I know, but I still feel bad when they’re all talking and I’m just standing there. I wish I could be part of it without feeling so awkward.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That makes sense—you want to feel included, not just be told that quiet is okay. What’s usually happening right before you start feeling awkward?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’m so tired of this quarantine dragging on. Every week feels the same, and I’m getting angry over nothing. Or maybe it’s not nothing. I don’t know.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds exhausting, and the anger may be telling you how much this is wearing on you. What’s been getting under your skin most lately?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It’s the feeling that there’s no end to it. I wake up, do the same stuff, and then it’s night again. I used to think I’d get used to it, but I haven’t.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That endless sameness can make each day feel heavy, especially when you’d hoped it would get easier. You don’t have to force yourself to be used to it. What do you miss most from your old routine?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I miss seeing people without planning it like some whole event. Just bumping into someone, sitting somewhere, hearing normal noise. Now I can go days barely talking to anyone, and I feel sort of invisible.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Feeling invisible makes sense when ordinary, spontaneous contact has disappeared. I’m glad you told me. What kind of small, low-effort contact feels most like what you’re missing?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Honestly, I’m not sure. Maybe just someone texting because they thought of me, not because we scheduled a check-in. I don’t want to have to ask people to remember I exist.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It hurts to want to feel remembered without having to organize it yourself. You deserve to feel seen, and I’m here with you right now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah. I appreciate that. I’m just tired of having to make everything happen myself. Even reaching out feels like another task I’m failing at.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds like a lot to carry—the loneliness, and the pressure to fix it yourself. Reaching out feeling hard doesn’t mean you’re failing. We can just stay with that for a moment.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep thinking, if I stopped trying, would anyone notice? I don’t mean I have a plan to hurt myself. I just feel so worn down and forgotten.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: I’m glad you told me. Are you thinking of ending your life? You can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any time. I hear that you feel worn down and forgotten, even without a plan to hurt yourself.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’m really worried I won’t have a job after Christmas. The company was counting on that new funding, and now… I don’t know what happens if it doesn’t come through.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That uncertainty sounds really unsettling, especially when so much depends on funding you can’t control. What feels most worrying about what might happen if it doesn’t come through?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That I won’t be able to keep up with rent. I’ve been there a while, and I don’t even know if I should start looking for something else or if that would make things worse here.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It makes sense that rent is the part that feels most urgent, and that looking elsewhere could feel like a risk to the job you have. What worries you most about starting to look?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I guess I’m afraid they’ll find out and think I’m not committed. And then I’ll lose the job sooner. But if I wait and the funding doesn’t come through, I could be stuck with nothing.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re caught between protecting the job you have and trying not to be left without options. That’s a hard position to sit in. What would help you feel a little clearer about your options right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe knowing when they’ll actually decide about the funding. My manager just says they’re waiting, and I can’t tell if that means a week or months. I don’t want to push too hard and seem difficult.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Not knowing the timeline seems to be keeping you on edge, and asking for clarity feels risky. What would you most want your manager to understand about why the timing matters to you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’d want them to know I need some warning to plan, especially with rent. I’m not asking them to promise me anything. I just hate feeling like I’m waiting for a decision that could change everything.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like you’re not asking for certainty, just enough notice to make a plan. That’s a reasonable thing to want. Would it help to think through a low-pressure way to ask your manager for a clearer timeline?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe. I could ask if they have any estimate, even a rough one, and say I’m trying to plan financially. I still feel nervous they’ll take it the wrong way. But waiting without asking is making me feel worse.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds like a thoughtful, straightforward way to ask. The nerves make sense, and it also sounds like having some information matters more than staying silent. Would it help to practice how you might say it?
